Isaac Newton. An English mathematician, physicist, and astronomer from sixteen forty-two to seventeen twenty-seven. His Principia Mathematica, published in sixteen eighty-seven, founded modern mechanics and gravitation theory and changed the course of science forever.

He independently developed calculus—his approach called the method of fluxions—to solve problems in physics. Leibniz independently developed it at the same time with better notation, creating a bitter priority dispute that dominated eighteenth-century mathematics. Newton's approach treated derivatives as rates of change of flowing quantities. The binomial theorem allows you to expand expressions like a plus b to the nth power as a power series without multiplying it out directly. His inverse square law relates gravitational force to the product of the masses divided by the square of the distance between them—the foundation of his theory of gravity.

The three laws of motion—the law of inertia, F equals ma, and the law of action-reaction—form the foundation of all classical mechanics. Universal gravitation was his crowning synthesis: it unified terrestrial and celestial mechanics into one system. The same force that drops an apple also keeps the Moon in orbit and governs the motions of the planets. He argued that gravity acts at a distance, instantaneously, without a mechanical medium carrying the force. Critics attacked this as "action at a distance," a seemingly magical concept, but Newton held firm.

He demonstrated that white light is composed of a spectrum of colours, each with a fixed refractivity, visible when light passes through a prism. He discovered that each colour bends a different amount when refracted, a phenomenon called dispersion. He invented the reflecting telescope, a mirror-based design, to avoid the chromatic aberration that plagued lens-based telescopes. His work in alchemy and theology was extensive, though unpublished in his lifetime and often eclipsed by his scientific legacy.

Newton stands at the hinge of the Scientific Revolution. He synthesised the work of Kepler, Galileo, and Descartes, and created a mathematical framework so powerful it shaped physics until Einstein. His insistence that mathematical laws govern nature, and that observation and experiment must validate them, became the gold standard for science. The calculus he developed became the language of all subsequent physics, engineering, and quantitative science. His reputation was so towering that eighteenth-century physicists hesitated to challenge Newtonian gravity even when problems hinted at cracks in the theory. Yet his methods remained vindicated for more than two hundred years.
